texts.preamble: Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 In The Court Of Sh. Harjyot Singh Bhalla Additional Sessions Judge-04 Patiala House Courts, New Delhi In The Matter Of: Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department Of Pfa & Anr Ca No. 117/2017 Cnr No. Dlnd01-000784-2017 Sh. Vishambar Dayal S/o Sh. Badri Prasad R/o 17/290, Kalyan Puri, Delhi-110091 ......Appellant Versus Department of P.F.A. Govt. of Nct of Delhi Nct of Delhi New Delhi ......Respondent Date of Institution: 21.01.2017 Date of decision : 12.01.2023 Judgment
texts.facts: 3. The brief facts of the case as per record and from trial court record are that accused is running an establishment namely M/s Aggarwal Provision and General Store, 13/80, Kalyanpuri, Delhi-91. On 01.07.2008 at about 07.00 p.m., Food Inspector Sh. VPS Chaudhary visited the said place and purchased 1500 grams of "Dal Arhar" (ready for sale) from accused. FI was accompanied with Field Assistant Sh. Jagdish Prasad and SDM/LHA Sh. Radha Charan. The said Dal Arhar was purchased for the purposes of analysis under PFA Act. The same sample was divided into three parts, packed as Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 1 per Rules of PFA. Panchanama was prepared. One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst. As per the report of Analyst, sample did not confirm to the standard because "The sample is coloured with synthetic colour viz. Tartrazine." 4. As the sample was failed, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 14.11.2008 with the court. Accused was summoned. He has exercised his right under Section 13(2) PFA Act by filing an application which was allowed by the court. 5. Charge was framed against accused under Section 2(ia) (j) & (m) read with Section 7 of PFA Act, 1954 punishable under Section 16(1A) of PFA Act. Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 2/20 6. Then I divided the sample into three equal parts by putting them in three clean and dry glass bottles separately. Then each sample bottle containing the sample was separately packed, Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 2 fastened, marked and sealed according to PFA Act and Rules." 11. Thereafter, PW-2 deposed as follows:- "Before taking the sample of Dal Arhar, it was properly mixed with the help of a clean and dry JHABA by rotating it in all possible directions. The so purchased quantity of sample commodity was divided then and there into three equal parts by putting it in three clean and dry glass bottles. All the three bottles containing the sample of Dal Arhar were separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed according to PFA Act and Rules." 12. PW-3 deposed in his examination in chief, which is as follows:- "The sample was lifted after proper mixing the Dal Arhar with the help of a clean and dry jhaba by rotating it in all possible directions several times. Then, so purchased quantity of sample commodity was divided into three equal parts by putting it into three clean and dry sample glass bottles. All the three sample bottles were separately sealed Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 4/20 and packed as per PFA Act & Rules." 13.
texts.arguments: The learned counsel for the appellant has submitted that in the present case, the conviction under the provisions of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is based on the finding of presence of synthetic colouring matter "Tartrazine" in the Dal sample collected from the shop of the convict/appellant. The learned counsel stated that he is restricting his arguments to the violation of Rule 14 of the PFA Rules, which provides the manner in which the sample is required to be collected by the Food Inspector and local health authority. 9. The learned counsel further stated that the appellant herein sells various articles and it was put to the witnesses on behalf of the appellant/convict and admitted by the witnesses that appellant was a retailer. The learned counsel submits that in the present case, Dal was allegedly lying in an open sack and sample was lifted with the help of a Jhaba, already lying at the shop of the appellant and weighed with the help of weighing pan being used by the appellant at his shop. Thereafter, it was placed in an envelope and from the envelope, the same was transferred in the glass bottles. Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 3/20 10. The learned counsel for the accused further submits that PW-1 had stated in his examination in chief that:- "The sample was taken after proper mixing Dal Arhar with the help of the dry and clean Jhaba lying by rotating it in all possible directions several times. Learned counsel for the appellant has stated that firstly, all the witnesses have simply admitted that the Jhaba lying at the store was used for mixing the Dal and lifting the sample. Learned counsel stated that there is no positive assertion by the witnesses regarding the compliance of Rule 14 as far as process of lifting of sample is concerned. Learned counsel has relied upon the decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Crl. L.P. 42/14 i.e. Delhi Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 7/20 Administration, through Designated Officer Vs. Rattan Lal, decided on 20.07.2014 and Food Inspector, Department of PFA Vs. Zahid 2014 (2) FAC 524 to submit that the officials were duty bound to clean the jhaba and the weighing Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 4 pan at the spot. It has been stated that SLP against the said decision in Delhi Administration Vs. Rattan Lal was also dismissed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court on 08.12.2014 being Crl. M.P. No. 23634/14. 20. Reliance is also being placed on the decision of Hon'ble Gujarat High Court in the case of State of Gujarat Vs. Laghadhirbhai Vaghijibhai Prajapati 2009 (2) 134 CCC (Gujarat), wherein, the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court analyzed the provisions contained in Rule 14 of the PF Rules and the relevant portion is quoted hereunder for ease of reference:- "7. However, on behalf of the respondent-accused, learned counsel Mr. Modi submitted that in the instant case, there is violation of Rule 14 of the Rules. Rule 14, pertains to manner of sending sample for analysis. It reads as under:- "14. Manner of sending samples for analysis:- Sample of food for the purpose of analysis shall be taken in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers, which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation, or in the case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed." Now, considering the provisions contained Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 8/20 in Rule 14 and appreciating the evidence on record, in the present case, it becomes clear that neither the Food Inspector Mr. Trivedi nor the panch Sanjay and nor the Sanitary Superintendent Kantilal Hargovinddas in their depositions clarified as to when, how and who cleaned the bottles, wherein the sample of groundnut oil was alleged to have been collected. It was submitted that mere oral statement of Food Inspector that the sample was collected in clean, dry bottles will not be termed as sufficient compliance of the mandatory requirements laid down under the Rules. In support thereof, the reliance has been placed upon a case of State of Gujarat v. Babu Luvji Jalia reported in 1997(2) FAC 26, wherein this High Court held that Rule 14 of the Rules lays down mandatory requirements and it is the duty of the prosecution to prove by leading positive evidence that bottles were cleaned and dried before the sample was taken by the Food Inspector. Reliance was also placed upon the judgment delivered by this court in the case of State of Gujarat v Sohanlal Trikamchand Shah reported in 2002(2) FAC 156, wherein almost identical principle was laid down as laid down in the above referred case. Reliance was also placed upon the case of State of Gujarat v. B.P.Prajapati reported in 2007(2) FAC 310, wherein referring to Rule 14 of the Rules in para-9 of said judgment, it was observed that "in fact Rule 14 makes it mandatory upon the prosecution to prove its due compliance by leading cogent and positive evidence. This Court is unable to agree with the submissions of Shri Patel that when the Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 9/20 Food Inspector has given his evidence that cleaned bottles were used, that itself is sufficient for establishing due compliance with provisions of Rule 14. Mere statement with regard to using clean bottles for collecting sample is not sufficient, as this court has held time and again." Under such circumstances, even mere statement. of the Food Inspector that the sample was collected in clean and dry bottle, would not amount to sufficient compliance of Rule 14. Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 5 8. Learned counsel Mr. Modi for the respondent-accused further submitted that perusing the evidence on record, it becomes clear that at the time of visiting the shop of the accused, the Food Inspector had carried with him the utensil called "tapeli", and the sample of groundnut oil from a tin containing the oil was collected with the help of "pali" an aluminium container or small utensil, which normally is used to take out loose edible oil from main container. It is submitted that even so far as the said "tapeli" and "pali" are concerned, there is no oral evidence worth the name that the same were clean or dry, much less any positive evidence in this respect. Considering the deposition of Food Inspector Mr.Sumanchandra Trivedi and Sanitary Superintendent Kantilal Hargovinddas, so far as "tapeli" and "pali" are concerned, there is no oral evidence adduced by them that the said utensils were clean and dry. Reliance was placed upon the case of Kliengar Dhana Rabari v. State of Gujarat decided on 08.02.1979 in Criminal Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 10/20 Revision Application No.447 of 1978 by this Court, wherein the sample of milk was collected by the Food Inspector and before dividing the sample into 3 different bottles, the milk was collected in a tumbler and this Court observed that the Food Inspector in his entire deposition, nowhere mentioned that the container i.e., tumbler in which the sample was taken, was clean and dry. Reliance was placed upon the case of State of Gujarat v. Laljibhai Ishwarbhai Zala decided on 15.02.2007 in Criminal Appeal No.841 of 2003, wherein the sample of edible oil was collected by the Food Inspector with the help of "pali" and it was observed that there was no evidence whatsoever that the same was clean, prior to taking out the sample from the main container. The learned counsel Mr.Modi for the respondent-accused relied upon the case of State of Maharashtra v. Vinayak Mahadeorao Waze reported in 2005 Cri. LJ 2100, wherein the sample of groundnut oil was collected by the Food Inspector and was divided into 3 glass bottles. Bombay High Court observing that the bottles in which the samples were collected, were not cleaned and dried in presence of accused and panch witnesses and held that the sample cannot be said to have been properly collected. In the case on hand, the non- compliance of the requirements laid down under Rule 14 of the Rules is clear." 21. The learned counsel has also relied upon the decision of Hon'ble Gauhati High Court in the case of Shew Chandar Mathur & Another Vs. State of Assam & Another, Criminal Revision No. 221 of 1984, decided on 29.08.1990, wherein, observations have been made on Rule 14 and the relevant portion is as follows:- "Rule 14 of the Rules provides for the manner in which sample is to be taken by the Food Inspector. It reads: Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 6 Samples of food for the purpose of analysis shall be taken in clean, dry bottles, or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation or in the case of dry substance entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed. The provision is intended to assure fair play and to exclude probability of an analysis which is not true in regard to ingredients of food stuff analyzed. It is mandatory and not directory. The conviction and sentence impugned in this petition should not be sustained." 22. Lastly, reliance has also been placed on the decision of Hon'ble Bombay High Court in the case of State of Maharashtra Vs. Bhaskar Rajeshwar Gangshettiwar & Ors. 2004 (I) FAC 13 to buttress the argument that the Food Inspector is duty bound to clean the container as also dry the same lest it is taken as non-conformity with the procedure laid down under PFA Rules. It is submitted that the same would apply to any article i.e. jhaba or weighing pan with which the article in question may come in contact during the process of taking of the sample. The Hon'ble Bombay High Court in fact notes that if Rule 14 is not followed, then the report of public analyst would lose its significance. 23. The learned counsel further submits that the aforesaid lapse in collection of sample has to be seen in the light of other defects in conduct of proceedings i.e. no public person was joined in the process, thereby, violating Rule 10. The learned counsel has lastly stated that the sentence in the present case is too harsh considering the age and long time taken in the trial of the present case as also the fact that food articles were not rendered unsafe by the presence of the alleged colour and it is a Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 13/20 mitigating factor. The proposition that the food articles were not rendered unsafe, is not in dispute, as per the learned counsel for the department. For this purpose, Ld. counsel for appellant had relied on Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 16/20 Judgment i.e. Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan, (Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203) of Hon. Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry, 1983 (1) SCC 177. 33. On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. SPP for the Department that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged. 35. As far as the application of Nemi Chand judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 17/20 T. Barai (supra) of Hon. Supreme Court. The relevant portion of the T. Barai judgment is as follows:- (Para 25) - It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment, or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication. In Michell v. Brown [(1958) 120 ER 909, 912: 32 LTOS 146 : 7 WR 80] Lord Campbell put the matter thus: "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an offence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute; see also Smith v. Benabo [(1937) 1 All ER 523: (1937) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194] . 36. In Regina v. Youle [(1861) 158 ER 311, 315-16: 4 LT 299: 9 WR 637], Martin, B. said in the oft-quoted passage: Vishambar Dayal vs . Department Of Pfa on 12 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15823858/ 9 "If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offences, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act." Moreover this particular aspect is stated as a illustration Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 18/20 in the same judgment in para 23 which is as follows:- To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life , then it cannot be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
